steps/4.description: The shared downstream lesion is loss of transcriptional control over extracellular matrix components, particularly the fibrillar collagens. Thinning is most pronounced centrally, with the periphery relatively preserved. The same matrix deficiency produces protrusion (keratoglobus, keratoconus), scleral thinning visible as blue sclerae, and axial elongation manifesting as high myopia.

open_questions/0.rationale: This entry lumps, and the reasoning should be auditable rather than assumed. In favour of lumping: the two genes were shown to participate in the same regulatory pathway; the downstream lesion, transcriptional dysregulation of fibrillar collagens, is shared; the clinical feature list and the management plan in the definitive review are stated once for BCS rather than per gene; and dismech's own rule is that a disorder entry needs one reasonably conserved pathograph, which BCS has. In favour of splitting: MONDO models them as two distinct children, and ZNF469 and PRDM5 are not the same molecule, so a gene-level query answers differently depending on the choice. That objection is addressed here by giving each subtype its own subtype_term, so both MONDO IDs remain curated and queryable without duplicating a pathograph that does not differ. If future work demonstrates a genotype-phenotype difference between BCS1 and BCS2 - none is currently described - splitting would become the better model.

A human-relevant New Approach Methodology assay — patient iPSC-cardiomyocytes and heterologous Nav1.5 expression subjected to a temperature ramp — directly measures the temperature-dependent INa loss that underlies fever unmasking, and is the mechanistic complement to the population EHR arm.

evidence.snippet: After comprehensive review by the clinical domain Expert panel, all 20 genes classified as limited evidence were reclassified as disputed with regard to any assertions of disease causality for BrS.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the disputed classification covers the whole non-SCN5A set rather than SCN3B alone, which is what makes this a stratum-level gap.

open_questions/1.rationale: Twenty of the twenty-one genes curated by the reappraisal are classified as disputed, and the founding reports for most of them, SCN3B included, were sporadic cases without informative segregation data or demonstrated rare-variant excess. That leaves the numbered MONDO series (Brugada syndrome 2 through 9) naming gene-specific entities whose gene-disease claims the field does not currently support. This entry already models the majority stratum as genotype-negative or oligogenic; what remains open is the status of these specific reported genes within it, that is, whether any individual one is a weak-effect contributor or simply not a Brugada gene at all. SCN3B is the concrete test case: its null mouse does produce reduced ventricular sodium current and inducible ventricular tachycardia, yet the specific human alleles reported for it are commoner in the population than the disease is, and one of them was also reported in lone atrial fibrillation. Resolving this determines whether this entry should ever carry gene-specific subtypes beyond SCN5A.

evidence.snippet: Together, these findings associate the lack of the Scn3b gene with arrhythmic tendencies in intact perfused hearts and electrophysiological features similar to those in Scn5a(+/-) hearts.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the strong model-side phenotype that makes the contrast with the human allele frequencies a genuine mismatch rather than a simple absence of model support.

evidence.snippet: Two curated genes in this study were originally implicated on the basis of variants suggested to be rare in the original studies, only to be subsequently noted to have heterozygosity frequency in public databases greater than or equal to the prevalence of BrS (KCNJ8 p.Ser422Leu, 1/250; SCN3B p.Leu10Pro, p.Val110Ile, both 1/2500).
evidence.explanation: The human-side half of the mismatch: the specific reported alleles are too common to cause the disease, whatever the null mouse shows.

open_questions/2.rationale: The in vivo model and the human genetics point in opposite directions, and the mismatch is at the level of the allele rather than the mechanism. Scn3b-null mice have reduced peak sodium current in ventricular myocytes, shortened ventricular effective refractory periods, and inducible ventricular tachycardia that the authors read as resembling Scn5a heterozygous hearts, so loss of beta-3 plainly can produce a sodium-channel-dependent ventricular arrhythmic substrate. But the model is a homozygous null, while every reported human variant is heterozygous, and two of them occur in the general population at roughly the prevalence of Brugada syndrome itself. So a strong model phenotype coexists with human alleles that cannot carry the disease at the frequency observed. Either the reported missense alleles do not approach the functional severity of a null, or beta-3 loss contributes only as a modifier on other substrate. Which of those holds determines whether the disputed classification is a statement about SCN3B or only about the specific alleles so far reported, and a heterozygous knock-in of the human alleles is the experiment that would separate them. Note that this discussion_id predates the question it now asks: it was first written around an apparent atrial-versus-ventricular mismatch that the Hakim 2008 ventricular data disproved. The id is retained as a stable key and should not be read as the claim.

evidence.snippet: We identified three unrelated individuals with de novo missense variants in CDK19
evidence.explanation: Human case-level evidence for the de novo disorder.

evidence.snippet: kinase activity of protein was lower for p.Gly28Arg and higher for p.Tyr32His substitutions compared with that of the wild-type protein.
evidence.explanation: Opposite biochemical effects do not support a uniformly decreased activity annotation.

genes/0.notes: G2P classifies the autosomal dominant CDK19–DEE87 relationship as Strong (evaluated 14 January 2025; GenCC SGC-123798.1). ClinGen has not published its own CDK19 validity curation. An earlier pericentric chromosome-6 inversion disrupted CDK19 and reduced transcript abundance in a patient with retinal folds, microcephaly and milder intellectual disability; that single structural case does not establish that all deletions or truncating alleles cause the missense-associated syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Current antiepileptic medications include daily valproic acid and clonazepam as needed.
evidence.explanation: Documented regimen; seizure control remained incomplete.

evidence.snippet: Currently, a combination of sodium valproate, topiramate, and lamotrigine are being used.
evidence.explanation: Combination use does not isolate efficacy of any one agent.

evidence.snippet: At 16 months of age, levetiracetam was added but was ineffective.
evidence.explanation: Negative evidence for successful seizure control in the reported individual; it does not establish lack of benefit in every patient.

evidence.snippet: oral treatment with topiramate was able to alleviate seizures for a few months
evidence.explanation: Temporary partial benefit; refractory seizures subsequently persisted.

treatments/0.description: Antiseizure regimens are individualized. Reported agents include valproate, clonazepam, topiramate, levetiracetam and lamotrigine, often in combination. Some patients remain drug resistant; a transient partial response to topiramate in the Thr31Asn case does not establish sustained or allele-specific efficacy.

evidence.snippet: Parenteral adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) injections and oral antiepileptic drugs, including sodium valproate and topiramate, failed to control the seizures.
evidence.explanation: Negative evidence for successful seizure control in the reported individual; it does not establish lack of benefit in every patient.

evidence.snippet: After he was given ACTH for 1 week, the drug was stopped because of a concomitant infection and immunosuppression concerns.
evidence.explanation: Treatment was interrupted for infection and immunosuppression concerns, so this observation does not establish efficacy or inefficacy.

treatments/1.description: ACTH was tried for infantile spasms or severe early epilepsy. It failed to control seizures in one Thr196Ala child and was stopped after one week in a Tyr32His child because of an intercurrent infection and immunosuppression concerns. The latter is a tolerability/interruption observation, not proof of inefficacy.

evidence.snippet: Her seizures had previously responded well to a ketogenic diet.
evidence.explanation: Reported benefit in one patient.

evidence.snippet: A ketogenic diet was tried but did not help to control seizures.
evidence.explanation: Negative evidence for successful seizure control in the reported individual; it does not establish lack of benefit in every patient.

evidence.snippet: Her epilepsy was refractory to conventional antiepileptic drugs and ketogenic diet.
evidence.explanation: Negative evidence for successful seizure control in the reported individual; it does not establish lack of benefit in every patient.

treatments/2.description: Responses differ between reported cases. The adult Thr196Ala patient previously responded well, whereas another Thr196Ala child and the Tyr32His CSF case had no adequate seizure response. These uncontrolled observations do not identify a uniformly effective or ineffective diet.

evidence.snippet: Oral dextromethorphan administration was initiated at 4 years of age but was unsuccessful.
evidence.explanation: Negative evidence for successful seizure control in the reported individual; it does not establish lack of benefit in every patient.

treatments/3.description: An NMDA-receptor antagonist was used at age four years in the Tyr32His patient with elevated CSF and plasma glycine, without clinical success. This is not an established treatment for CDK19-related disorder, and a glycine-driven mechanism remains unconfirmed.

evidence.snippet: we supplemented NACA into the fly medium at a concentration of 80 μg/ml and raised all flies on NACA supplemented food for the entirety of their lifecycle
evidence.explanation: Experimental fly exposure, not a human dose recommendation.

evidence.snippet: there is no significant difference in the adult IFM myofibril width from adults raised with or without NACA supplementation
evidence.explanation: No structural myofibril rescue; this separate readout does not refute the measured ROS reduction.

treatments/4.description: Dietary N-acetylcysteine amide (NACA), distinct from N-acetylcysteine, reduced muscle ROS in Thr196Ala-expressing flies and shortened mitochondria across all tested genotypes. Myofibril width was not rescued. The proportion reaching the climbing endpoint did not significantly improve, although per-assay climbing distributions showed mild improvement. No human efficacy or seizure benefit was tested.

evidence.snippet: expression of T196A is contributing to elevated muscular ROS that NACA can suppress
evidence.explanation: Model-specific antioxidant effect.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Reduced DHE fluorescence in the sensitized Thr196Ala fly background; human translation is untested.

evidence.snippet: She walked at 5 years of age with the help of orthotics.
evidence.explanation: Individual mobility-support observation.

treatments/5.description: Care addresses developmental, communication and mobility needs. Orthotics helped the adult founding patient attain walking at age five; that observation does not establish the efficacy of a specific rehabilitation protocol.

evidence.snippet: We identified three unrelated individuals with de novo missense variants in CDK19
evidence.explanation: De novo case evidence informs counseling; this is not a measured recurrence-risk estimate.

treatments/6.description: Variant interpretation and parental testing inform counseling. Most reported missense cases are de novo, but a negative parental blood result does not exclude germline mosaicism. A quantitative recurrence or penetrance estimate is not established by these reports.

evidence.snippet: kinase activity of protein was lower for p.Gly28Arg and higher for p.Tyr32His substitutions compared with that of the wild-type protein.
evidence.explanation: Variant catalytic assay.

evidence.snippet: both variants are unable to rescue the cdk8 depletion muscle myofibril thickening as the wild-type CDK19 can
evidence.explanation: Readout-specific persistent defect.

open_questions/0.rationale: Tyr32His increases catalytic output in biochemical assays while its rescue varies across fly tissues, temperatures and residual ortholog expression. Failed complementation, overexpression toxicity and reduced catalytic activity are distinct observations. Dominant-negative interaction with the normal human allele remains unproven.

evidence.snippet: These results show that cytoplasmic CDK19 is sufficient to regulate mitochondrial morphology.
evidence.explanation: Model evidence underlying the translational gap.

open_questions/1.rationale: Cytoplasmic rescue and patient-variant fly experiments support a route beyond transcription. Patient-neuron mitochondrial morphology, phosphorylation and energy defects have not been established in these studies. NACA effects in flies provide a hypothesis for further testing, not a validated human therapy.

evidence.snippet: The mechanism through which the CDK19 variant leads to the CSF abnormalities remains unknown.
evidence.explanation: Explicit uncertainty in the primary report.

open_questions/2.rationale: These biochemical findings come from one Tyr32His case. A normal CSF/plasma ratio, negative GLDC/AMT testing and unsuccessful dextromethorphan treatment limit an NKH-like mechanistic interpretation. Replication and direct metabolic studies are needed before these values can be used as diagnostic or treatment biomarkers.

evidence.snippet: The transcript level for CDK19 in the patient was found to be 54% (p = 0.022) when compared with the control mean
evidence.explanation: Inversion-associated RNA decrease.

open_questions/3.rationale: The pericentric inversion was mapped to CDK19 intron 1 and reduced transcript levels in transformed lymphoblasts, supporting a dosage effect. Retinal folds, microcephaly and milder intellectual disability without reported epilepsy differ from many missense cases. Breakpoint mapping did not establish a nucleotide-resolved junction, and the isolated structural case does not establish pathogenicity of all CDK19 deletions or truncations.

evidence.snippet: We describe a new Type II congenital disorder of glycosylation (CDG-II) caused by mutations in the conserved oligomeric Golgi (COG) complex gene, COG8.
evidence.explanation: Establishes COG8 as the causal gene.

steps/1.description: Biallelic COG8 variants impair function of a lobe B component of the conserved oligomeric Golgi complex. Published genotypes include nonsense, frameshift and splice-altering alleles. Their cellular effects vary: absence of detectable COG8 and residual truncated protein have both been reported.

evidence.snippet: Patient fibroblasts completely lacked COG8 protein and had reduced levels and/or mislocalization of several other COG proteins.
evidence.explanation: Undetectable protein in this particular patient line.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, compared with control, only 25% of the immunoreactivity was recovered, suggesting that the transcript or the truncated Cog8 protein is unstable
evidence.explanation: Residual truncated protein in the p.Tyr537Ter line limits a universal null-protein claim.

steps/2.description: COG8 was undetectable in the compound-heterozygous patient fibroblasts reported by Kranz et al. In the p.Tyr537Ter patient, a truncated protein remained detectable at about one quarter of control immunoreactivity. These are genotype-specific fibroblast measurements, not proof of complete absence in all tissues.

evidence.snippet: As a result, Cog1 deficiency accompanies the Cog8 deficiency, preventing assembly of the intact, stable complex and resulting in the appearance of smaller subcomplexes.
evidence.explanation: The interaction and fractionation studies identify a defect in complex integrity.

evidence.snippet: Although weaker in immunofluorescence signal, as expected from the western blot analysis, the Cog1 subunit was associated with the Golgi in both the patient and control fibroblasts
evidence.explanation: Retained localization in the p.Tyr537Ter patient prevents equating reduced COG1 abundance with loss from the Golgi in every genotype.

evidence.snippet: In CDG-derived Cog8-deficient fibroblasts, Cog1 was not detected in the Golgi
evidence.explanation: Contrasting result in the patient line studied by Laufman et al.

steps/3.description: The p.Tyr537Ter truncation disrupts the COG1-COG8 interaction and intact complex assembly. Smaller subcomplexes remain. Secondary COG1 reduction is not uniform absence: COG1 remained weakly Golgi-localized in the p.Tyr537Ter patient, whereas it was not detected at the Golgi in the other patient line used in the 2013 study.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, levels of beta1,4-galactosytransferase were significantly reduced.
evidence.explanation: Reduced enzyme abundance in the patient-cell study.

steps/4.description: Beta1,4-galactosyltransferase abundance was reduced in the p.Tyr537Ter patient fibroblasts despite retained perinuclear localization. Abundance, localization and catalytic activity are distinct readouts; this experiment does not quantify a disease-wide enzyme deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Analysis of serum transferrin and total serum N-glycans showed normal addition of one sialic acid, but severe deficiency in subsequent sialylation of mostly normal N-glycans.
evidence.explanation: Serum finding in one patient.

evidence.snippet: Mass spectrometric analysis of the N- and O-glycan structures identified a mild sialylation deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Biochemically mild result does not imply absence of major neurological disability.

evidence.snippet: Surprisingly, the data also show a minor increase in sialylation in the N-glycans of COG6- and COG8-deficient cells.
evidence.explanation: Total-cell HeLa N-glycans differ from patient serum findings; the model does not reproduce this readout.

steps/5.description: Serum N-glycans and transferrin show incomplete terminal sialylation, with biochemical severity varying between cases. The markedly impaired addition of subsequent sialic acids described by Kranz et al. is not an invariant pattern in all genotypes. Acute COG8 knockdown in HeLa cells instead produced a minor increase in total cellular N-glycan sialylation.

evidence.snippet: Mass spectrometric analysis of the N- and O-glycan structures identified a mild sialylation deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Serum glycan analysis confirms the O-glycan component.

evidence.snippet: The defects in O-glycosylation could be fully restored by transfecting the patient's fibroblasts with full-length Cog8.
evidence.explanation: Complementation supports a COG8-dependent cellular phenotype.

steps/6.description: Patient serum O-glycan analysis, ApoC-III isoelectric focusing and fibroblast lectin assays identify an O-glycosylation defect. In the p.Tyr537Ter patient, wild-type COG8 complementation reduced abnormal PNA staining. This is cellular rescue, not a demonstrated clinical gene therapy.

evidence.snippet: the interactions of Stx5 with either the v-SNARE GS15 or the t-SNAREs Ykt6 and GS28 were significantly reduced in both Cog8-deficient cell types.
evidence.explanation: NEM-stabilized immunoprecipitation detects reduced Stx5 complex assembly.

evidence.snippet: Despite the differences in the steady-state distributions of the SNARE proteins, the assembly of the Stx6 SNARE complex was impaired in both Cog8-deficient cell types.
evidence.explanation: Independent Stx6 complex assembly readout in both systems.

steps/7.description: Assembly of the Stx5-GS28-Ykt6-GS15 and Stx6-Stx16-Vti1a-VAMP4 complexes is reduced in COG8-depleted HeLa cells and the tested COG8-CDG fibroblasts. Protein abundance and localization differ between the systems; loss of complex assembly is not identical to loss of every SNARE protein.

evidence.snippet: Patient fibroblasts were deficient in sialylation of both N- and O-glycans, and also showed slower brefeldin A (BFA)-induced disruption of the Golgi matrix, reminiscent of COG7-deficient cells.
evidence.explanation: Patient-cell BFA redistribution result.

evidence.snippet: In the patient's cells, however, the BFA-induced redistribution of Golgi mannosidase II was significantly delayed at all times investigated
evidence.explanation: The p.Tyr537Ter line also has a delayed BFA response.

steps/8.description: Patient fibroblasts exhibit delayed brefeldin A-induced redistribution of Golgi proteins. This pharmacological assay supports abnormal retrograde trafficking; it does not directly measure every physiological intra-Golgi transport step.

evidence.snippet: depletion of the Cog8 subunit substantially inhibited the transport of TGN38-HA to the TGN in HeLa cells.
evidence.explanation: Dynamic transport measurement is specific to the HeLa model.

evidence.snippet: Collectively, these results suggest that Cog8 deficiency in either HeLa cells or CDG-derived fibroblasts influences endosome-to-TGN retrograde transport.
evidence.explanation: Patient localization data support, but do not duplicate, the HeLa kinetic evidence.

steps/9.description: COG8-depleted HeLa cells show delayed TGN38 antibody-uptake trafficking to the trans-Golgi network. Patient fibroblasts show altered endogenous TGN38/46 and CI-MPR distribution, supporting disturbed recycling but without the same kinetic assay in patient cells.

evidence.snippet: In all analyzed COG KD cells, MGAT1, MAN2A1 and ST6GAL1 proteins were found in multiple vesicle-like structures, as well as in large fragmented Golgi mini-stacks that were positive for the Golgi matrix protein GM130.
evidence.explanation: The tested panel included COG8-depleted HeLa cells.

evidence.snippet: Both enzymes appeared to exhibit a normal perinuclear Golgi distribution in the patient's cells
evidence.explanation: Mannosidase II and beta1,4-galactosyltransferase localization counterexample in p.Tyr537Ter fibroblasts.

steps/10.description: In COG8 siRNA-depleted HeLa cells, tested Golgi enzymes redistribute to vesicle-like structures and fragmented Golgi. This is not universal in patient fibroblasts: mannosidase II and beta1,4-galactosyltransferase retained perinuclear Golgi distribution in the p.Tyr537Ter patient. Effects depend on the protein, genotype and cell system.

steps/5.description: Cadmium enters the body via inhalation of fumes/dust or gastrointestinal absorption from contaminated food and water. Inhaled cadmium is absorbed considerably more efficiently than ingested cadmium, and gastrointestinal uptake is enhanced by iron deficiency via the shared divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1). Once absorbed, cadmium distributes via the bloodstream bound to albumin and accumulates in liver, kidney, and bone with a biological half-life of 10-30 years.

evidence.snippet: soluble compounds of definite carcinogenic metals and metalloids, such as arsenic, cadmium and nickel, and putative carcinogens, including cobalt and lead, inhibit zinc finger containing DNA repair proteins
evidence.explanation: Cell-culture and ex vivo work showing cadmium inhibits zinc-finger-containing DNA repair proteins, the molecular lesion this node models.

evidence.snippet: Zinc fingers can thus be compromised by a substitution of Zn(II) with another metal ion
evidence.explanation: States the substitution mechanism - a competing divalent cation replacing the structural Zn(II) - that makes cadmium a zinc-finger poison.

evidence.snippet: The epigenetic effects of Cd, including DNA methylation and histone modifications, are also explored to explain its long-term impact on gene expression and disease manifestation
evidence.explanation: Review situating cadmium's epigenetic dysregulation alongside the genotoxic arm as a second route to long-term altered gene expression. Evidence source is OTHER because this is a review article.

steps/6.description: Cadmium is a weak direct mutagen; its genotoxicity is largely indirect and runs through the zinc-finger fold. Cd(2+) substitutes for the structural Zn(II) held tetrahedrally by cysteine thiolates and histidine imidazoles in zinc-finger domains, and cadmium-driven oxidative stress independently oxidises those thiolate donors. Because several DNA-repair proteins (nucleotide-excision and mismatch-repair components) are zinc-finger proteins, the displacement inhibits repair without altering the underlying gene sequence - a loss-of-function-like lesion imposed on the proteome rather than encoded in the genome. This node is the mechanistic bridge from the systemic cadmium burden to the carcinogenic arm, and is why cadmium behaves as a co-mutagen and repair inhibitor rather than as a classical DNA-adduct-forming carcinogen.

evidence.snippet: This half-life is partly as a result of metallothioneins (MTs), metal-binding proteins with a high affinity for Cd.
evidence.explanation: Confirms metallothionein as the primary cadmium-binding protein responsible for cadmium's long biological half-life.

evidence.snippet: The kidney is the main organ affected by chronic Cd exposure and toxicity. Cd accumulates in the kidney as a result of its preferential uptake by receptor-mediated endocytosis of freely filtered and metallothionein bound Cd (Cd-MT) in the renal proximal tubule.
evidence.explanation: Review confirms that hepatically-produced Cd-MT is filtered and taken up by the kidney, establishing the liver-to-kidney transfer pathway.

steps/7.description: The liver is the primary site of initial cadmium detoxification. Hepatocytes synthesize metallothionein (MT), a cysteine-rich protein that binds cadmium with high affinity. The cadmium-metallothionein (Cd-MT) complex is slowly released into the bloodstream over time. While MT binding initially protects against free cadmium toxicity, the Cd-MT complex is filtered at the glomerulus and taken up by renal tubular cells, effectively transferring the cadmium burden to the kidney.

evidence.snippet: the multiligand endocytic receptors megalin and cubilin take up cadmium-metallothionein complexes via receptor-mediated endocytosis.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that megalin and cubilin receptors mediate the endocytic uptake of Cd-MT complexes in proximal tubule.

evidence.snippet: Cd2+ complexed to metallothionein (MT) (CdMT) is taken up through receptor-mediated endocytosis (RME) via the PT receptor megalin:cubilin, which is the predominant pathway for reuptake of filtered proteins in the kidney.
evidence.explanation: Confirms megalin:cubilin as the predominant receptor for Cd-MT uptake in proximal tubule.

evidence.snippet: Cd accumulates in the kidney as a result of its preferential uptake by receptor-mediated endocytosis of freely filtered and metallothionein bound Cd (Cd-MT) in the renal proximal tubule. Internalised Cd-MT is degraded in endosomes and lysosomes, releasing free Cd(2+) into the cytosol
evidence.explanation: Review details the full Cd-MT uptake pathway: glomerular filtration, receptor-mediated endocytosis, lysosomal degradation, and free Cd2+ release.

evidence.snippet: The high retention properties of the kidneys reside in proximal tubular cells that possess transport mechanisms for Cd-MT uptake, ultimately leading to more Cd accumulation.
evidence.explanation: Confirms proximal tubular cells possess specific transport mechanisms for Cd-MT uptake.

steps/8.description: The cadmium-metallothionein (Cd-MT) complex is freely filtered at the glomerulus because of its low molecular weight. Proximal tubular epithelial cells reabsorb Cd-MT via receptor-mediated endocytosis through the megalin/cubilin receptor complex. Once internalized, Cd-MT is degraded in lysosomes, releasing free cadmium ions intracellularly. This mechanism explains the kidney's particular vulnerability to cadmium accumulation.

evidence.snippet: We will present a case of cadmium induced peripheral neuropathy, nephropathy, and decreased bone density.
evidence.explanation: Documents reduced bone density in a cadmium-exposed patient. Marked PARTIAL: the same patient had nephropathy, so this single clinical observation cannot separate a direct bone-cell effect from the renal phosphate-wasting route, and cannot support the independence claim.

steps/9.description: A direct skeletal arm of cadmium toxicity is proposed alongside the renal phosphate-wasting route: cadmium is held to act on bone cells themselves, reducing osteoblast function and favouring osteoclastic resorption. The evidence currently curated here does NOT establish that arm — the only human observation available is reduced bone density in an occupationally exposed patient who also had nephropathy, so the renal route is not excluded and the claim of independence from phosphate wasting is not supported. Cell-level (osteoblast culture or animal) evidence is needed before this node asserts a direct mechanism; see the attached knowledge gap.

evidence.snippet: the environmental pollutant cadmium is known to increase the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin (IL)-6, IL-8, and chemokine (C-C motif) ligand 2 (CCL2) by activating the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) pathways.
evidence.explanation: In vitro study demonstrates cadmium activation of MAPK and NF-kB inflammatory pathways with cytokine secretion.

evidence.snippet: exercise, both before and during Cd exposure, can reduce Cd caused pathological damages in the liver and duodenum of mice, suppressing the expression levels of the IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α genes.
evidence.explanation: Mouse model confirms cadmium-induced expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α.

steps/10.description: Cadmium activates pro-inflammatory signaling cascades including the NF-kB and MAPK/JNK pathways, leading to increased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1beta, IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-8, CCL2) and upregulation of COX-2. This chronic inflammatory state exacerbates organ-specific injury in kidney, liver, and intestine.

evidence.snippet: She had chronic renal failure with a high Cd exposure level and advanced renal tubular dysfunction.
evidence.explanation: Documents advanced renal tubular dysfunction resulting from proximal tubular cell injury in chronic cadmium exposure.

evidence.snippet: Internalised Cd-MT is degraded in endosomes and lysosomes, releasing free Cd(2+) into the cytosol, where it can generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) and activate cell death pathways.
evidence.explanation: Review details the mechanism of tubular cell injury: lysosomal release of free Cd2+ generates ROS and activates apoptosis.

steps/11.description: When intracellular cadmium exceeds the metallothionein binding capacity of proximal tubular cells, free cadmium ions cause oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and activation of apoptotic pathways. Cadmium displaces zinc from zinc-finger proteins and disrupts calcium signaling, leading to tubular cell death.

evidence.snippet: We report the case of a 48-year-old man who presented with severe osteoporosis, impaired renal function and acquired Fanconi syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Case report confirming cadmium-induced acquired Fanconi syndrome with impaired tubular reabsorption.

evidence.snippet: Cd reduced the transcriptional expression of megalin and ClC5 and, at the same time, increased the degradation of megalin and ClC5 proteins via the lysosomal pathway in an in vitro model of renal proximal tubular cells.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the molecular mechanism: cadmium downregulates megalin and ClC5, the key receptors for protein reabsorption, explaining Fanconi syndrome.

evidence.snippet: The exposure of S1 and S2 cells to Cd at 1 and 3 µM for 3 days resulted in significant decreases in the uptakes of β2-MG and metallothionein but not in those of albumin or transferrin.
evidence.explanation: In vitro study directly demonstrates cadmium impairs endocytic uptake of low-molecular-weight proteins at nonlethal concentrations.

evidence.snippet: An early and sensitive manifestation of chronic Cd renal toxicity, which can be useful in individual and population screening, is impaired reabsorption of low molecular weight proteins (LMWP)
evidence.explanation: Review confirms impaired LMWP reabsorption as the earliest and most sensitive indicator of cadmium nephrotoxicity.

steps/12.description: Injury to proximal tubular cells causes Fanconi syndrome, characterized by impaired reabsorption of low-molecular-weight proteins (beta-2-microglobulin, retinol-binding protein), glucose, amino acids, uric acid, and phosphate. This is the earliest and most sensitive clinical indicator of chronic cadmium nephrotoxicity, detectable before decline in GFR.

evidence.snippet: liver SOD, GSH-Px, T-AOC and CAT levels were decreased, and MDA level was increased in Cd-treated goats, and 630 DEPs (up 326, down 304) in the livers of Cd-treated goats.
evidence.explanation: Proteomic study in goats confirms cadmium-induced hepatic antioxidant depletion.

evidence.snippet: exercise significantly decreased blood ALT and AST levels, alleviating oxidative stress in the liver by reducing MDA synthesis and enhancing SOD and GSH-PX activities.
evidence.explanation: Mouse model demonstrates cadmium-induced hepatic oxidative stress with depleted antioxidant enzymes.

evidence.snippet: Cd exposure altered hepatic lipid homeostasis via the perturbation of steatosis gene expression and lipid species abundances. Additionally, Cd exposure triggered a hepatic antioxidant response
evidence.explanation: Mouse model demonstrates cadmium triggers hepatic antioxidant response and disrupts lipid homeostasis, consistent with oxidative stress-driven liver injury.

steps/13.description: Cadmium disrupts the hepatic redox balance: animal studies show reduced activity of the antioxidant enzymes SOD, GSH-Px, and CAT together with increased lipid peroxidation (elevated MDA). Note the evidence curated here measures antioxidant ENZYME activity rather than glutathione stores themselves, and one study reports cadmium triggering a hepatic antioxidant RESPONSE - so "depletion" is the interpretation placed on these readouts, not a directly measured finding. The claim that cadmium alters cytochrome P450 drug metabolism is not evidenced in this entry.

evidence.snippet: Exercise inhibited nuclear damage and hepatocyte apoptosis caused by Cd by increasing Bcl-2 protein expression and preventing the release of pro-apoptotic proteins such as caspase-3, Cytc, Bax, caspase-8and cleaved-caspase-3.
evidence.explanation: Mouse model demonstrates cadmium-induced hepatocyte apoptosis via pro-apoptotic protein release.

steps/14.description: Sustained oxidative stress from glutathione depletion triggers hepatocyte apoptosis via mitochondrial pathways. Cadmium causes release of pro-apoptotic proteins (cytochrome c, caspase-3, Bax) and nuclear damage, leading to progressive hepatocellular loss and liver injury.

evidence.snippet: Three silversmiths presented similarly with clinical, biochemical and radiological evidence of hypophosphataemic osteomalacia.
evidence.explanation: Confirms hypophosphataemia from renal phosphate wasting as the driver of cadmium-induced osteomalacia.

steps/15.description: Impaired proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption leads to chronic phosphaturia and hypophosphataemia. The sustained phosphate loss is the primary metabolic driver of cadmium-induced osteomalacia, as phosphate is essential for hydroxyapatite crystal formation in bone.

evidence.snippet: She had chronic renal failure with a high Cd exposure level and advanced renal tubular dysfunction.
evidence.explanation: Documents progression to chronic renal failure from sustained cadmium-induced tubular damage.

evidence.snippet: Continued and heavy Cd exposure can progress to the clinical renal Fanconi syndrome, and ultimately to renal failure.
evidence.explanation: Review confirms the progressive nature of cadmium nephrotoxicity from tubular dysfunction to renal failure.

steps/16.description: Sustained proximal tubular injury from cadmium accumulation leads to tubulointerstitial inflammation, fibrosis, and progressive nephron loss. Glomerular filtration rate declines as tubulointerstitial nephritis advances, ultimately resulting in chronic kidney disease.

evidence.snippet: Three silversmiths presented similarly with clinical, biochemical and radiological evidence of hypophosphataemic osteomalacia.
evidence.explanation: Confirms defective bone mineralization causing osteomalacia in cadmium-exposed workers.

evidence.snippet: The shortening of height, bone deformities and fractures, abnormal bone metabolism suggesting osteomalacia, and renal anemia were also noted.
evidence.explanation: Documents skeletal consequences of defective mineralization in itai-itai disease.

steps/17.description: Chronic hypophosphataemia from renal phosphate wasting impairs hydroxyapatite crystal deposition in osteoid, causing osteomalacia. Bone becomes soft and prone to deformation and pathologic fractures. In itai-itai disease, severe demineralization causes fractures from minimal trauma, height loss, and skeletal deformities.

evidence.snippet: Cd exposure, even at a relatively low dosage (4 mg/L), significantly facilitates the progression of atherosclerosis in apolipoprotein E-deficient mice fed a high-fat diet. This pro-atherogenic effect was accompanied by comprehensive disturbances in systemic and vascular cholesterol homeostasis
evidence.explanation: Mouse model demonstrates cadmium promotes atherosclerosis through disruption of systemic and vascular cholesterol homeostasis, even at low doses.

evidence.snippet: we identified miR-30d-5p and miR-504-3p as novel epigenetic regulators mediating Cd-induced foam cell formation. Specifically, Cd treatment upregulated miR-30d-5p and downregulated miR-504-3p, which directly targeted NCEH1 and CD36, respectively, thereby promoting intracellular lipid accumulation.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the molecular mechanism: cadmium modulates specific miRNAs that regulate cholesterol handling genes, driving foam cell formation and atherosclerotic plaque development.

evidence.snippet: plasma miR-30d-5p levels were positively associated with Cd exposure and partially mediated the Cd-stroke association, accounting for 16.4% of the total effect.
evidence.explanation: Human case-control study (494 ischemic stroke patients vs 494 controls) validates miR-30d-5p as a mediator of cadmium-induced stroke risk.

steps/18.description: Cadmium disrupts cholesterol homeostasis in the vascular wall, promoting atherosclerosis through miRNA-mediated dysregulation of cholesterol uptake (CD36), efflux (ABCA1), and hydrolysis (NCEH1). Cadmium upregulates miR-30d-5p and downregulates miR-504-3p, promoting foam cell formation and intracellular lipid accumulation in macrophages. This pathway links cadmium exposure to increased cardiovascular risk, particularly ischemic stroke.

evidence.snippet: Cadmium (Cd) and its compounds were classified as "carcinogenic to humans (Group 1)" by IARC in 1993
evidence.explanation: Establishes the IARC Group 1 classification and its basis in cadmium-exposed worker cohorts.

evidence.snippet: Current data consistently suggest a causal role of exposure to cadmium in pancreas, lung, and bladder carcinogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Systematic review of 9 meta-analyses and 57 original articles giving the sites where a causal role is currently supported.

evidence.snippet: The association between cadmium exposure and prostate cancer was not confirmed in the latest available updates.
evidence.explanation: Carried as a qualification, not a refutation of the node: the same review that establishes the Group 1 classification withdraws support for the prostate site specifically, which is why site attribution here is not uniform.

steps/19.description: Cadmium and its compounds have been classified by IARC as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1) since 1993, on the strength of excess lung cancer in occupationally exposed cohorts together with animal tumour data. The contemporary evidence base, reviewed across biological-sample studies, supports a causal role at the lung, pancreas and bladder, with total cancer risk and mortality correlating with measured cadmium body burden. Site attribution is deliberately not curated uniformly: the prostate association was not confirmed on cohort update, and breast and prostate evidence remains weak or inconclusive. Latency is that of chemical carcinogenesis - years to decades - which is why this arm is a feature of chronic rather than acute cadmium poisoning.

evidence.snippet: She had chronic renal failure with a high Cd exposure level and advanced renal tubular dysfunction.
evidence.explanation: Documents renal tubular dysfunction as a key manifestation of chronic cadmium exposure.

evidence.snippet: We report the case of a 48-year-old man who presented with severe osteoporosis, impaired renal function and acquired Fanconi syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Confirms acquired Fanconi syndrome from chronic cadmium toxicity.

steps/20.description: Proximal renal tubular dysfunction manifesting as Fanconi syndrome with low-molecular-weight proteinuria (beta-2-microglobulinuria), glucosuria, aminoaciduria, and phosphaturia. The earliest and most sensitive indicator of chronic cadmium nephrotoxicity.

evidence.snippet: An early and sensitive manifestation of chronic Cd renal toxicity, which can be useful in individual and population screening, is impaired reabsorption of low molecular weight proteins (LMWP) (also a receptor-mediated process in the proximal tubule) such as retinol binding protein (RBP). This so-called 'tubular proteinuria' is a good index of proximal tubular damage
evidence.explanation: Review identifies LMW proteinuria as the earliest and most sensitive marker of cadmium nephrotoxicity, suitable for population screening.

evidence.snippet: Cadmium nephrotoxicity is heralded by increased excretion of beta2-microglobulin, retinol binding protein and alpha1-microglobulin, indicative of decreased proximal tubule function.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the specific LMW proteins excreted in cadmium nephrotoxicity: beta-2-microglobulin, retinol binding protein, and alpha-1-microglobulin.

steps/21.description: Increased urinary excretion of low-molecular-weight proteins (beta-2-microglobulin, retinol-binding protein, alpha-1-microglobulin) reflecting impaired proximal tubular reabsorption. A hallmark biomarker of cadmium nephrotoxicity used for screening in exposed populations.

evidence.snippet: Three silversmiths presented similarly with clinical, biochemical and radiological evidence of hypophosphataemic osteomalacia.
evidence.explanation: Confirms hypophosphataemic osteomalacia from occupational cadmium exposure.

evidence.snippet: The shortening of height, bone deformities and fractures, abnormal bone metabolism suggesting osteomalacia, and renal anemia were also noted.
evidence.explanation: Documents osteomalacia with bone deformities and fractures in itai-itai disease.

steps/22.description: Defective bone mineralization caused by cadmium-induced renal phosphate wasting, leading to hypophosphataemia. Presents with bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, waddling gait, and pathologic fractures.

evidence.snippet: We report the case of a 48-year-old man who presented with severe osteoporosis, impaired renal function and acquired Fanconi syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Case report of severe osteoporosis from chronic cadmium toxicity.

evidence.snippet: We will present a case of cadmium induced peripheral neuropathy, nephropathy, and decreased bone density.
evidence.explanation: Confirms decreased bone density (osteoporosis) from cadmium exposure.

steps/23.description: Decreased bone mineral density from combined effects of renal phosphate and calcium wasting, direct cadmium toxicity to osteoblasts, and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Contributes to pathologic fractures, particularly in chronic exposure.

evidence.snippet: a bone disease with fractures and severe pain, the itai-itai disease, a form of Cd-induced renal osteomalacia, was identified in Japan.
evidence.explanation: Historical review identifies severe bone pain as the defining symptom of itai-itai disease, the archetypal chronic cadmium poisoning syndrome.

evidence.snippet: during the last 12 years of his life the patient had suffered increasing disability from gross bone disease. Several bone biopsies and detailed metabolic studies showed typical severe osteomalacia
evidence.explanation: Case report documents 12 years of progressive bone pain and disability from cadmium-induced osteomalacia in an occupationally exposed worker.

steps/24.description: Severe bone pain, particularly in the legs, pelvis, and spine. The hallmark symptom of itai-itai disease (literally "it hurts, it hurts" disease). Results from osteomalacia and pathologic fractures.

evidence.snippet: Three silversmiths presented similarly with clinical, biochemical and radiological evidence of hypophosphataemic osteomalacia.
evidence.explanation: Confirms hypophosphataemia as the metabolic derangement underlying cadmium-induced osteomalacia.

steps/25.description: Low serum phosphate levels resulting from impaired proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption. A key driver of cadmium-induced osteomalacia and a diagnostic clue when found with renal tubular dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: She had chronic renal failure with a high Cd exposure level and advanced renal tubular dysfunction.
evidence.explanation: Documents chronic renal failure from cadmium exposure.

steps/26.description: Progressive decline in renal function from chronic cadmium accumulation. Glomerular filtration rate declines as tubular damage progresses to tubulointerstitial nephritis.

evidence.snippet: Heavy metal inhalation is a rare cause of acute lung injury. Among the various heavy metals, cadmium is more commonly known to cause acute lung injury.
evidence.explanation: Confirms cadmium as a cause of acute lung injury from inhalation.

evidence.snippet: For patients with concurrent lung and kidney involvement, mechanical ventilation and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) may be required.
evidence.explanation: Systematic review confirms severe pulmonary involvement requiring mechanical ventilation.

steps/27.description: Acute respiratory distress syndrome from cadmium fume inhalation. May be fatal and often presents with delayed onset after initial asymptomatic period. Requires mechanical ventilation and intensive care support.

evidence.explanation: Supports the dose-related nature of the association, measured as cadmium in blood, urine, nails or hair rather than as modelled exposure.

evidence.explanation: The Group 1 classification rests substantially on excess lung cancer in cadmium-exposed worker cohorts, which is why it is cited on this site.

steps/28.description: Excess lung cancer incidence and mortality in populations with elevated cadmium body burden. This is the site on which the IARC Group 1 designation principally rests, evidenced most strongly in occupationally exposed cohorts. Site attribution is deliberately split across three entries rather than asserted as one undifferentiated malignancy phenotype, because the evidence is site-specific: lung, pancreas and bladder are supported while breast and prostate explicitly are not. Onset follows the years-to-decades latency of chemical carcinogenesis, so this is a manifestation of chronic rather than acute cadmium poisoning. `frequency:` is omitted throughout: the underlying evidence is exposure-response association across heterogeneous cohorts, not a per-patient manifestation rate, so no FrequencyEnum band is justified.

evidence.snippet: By detailing the absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) of Cd, alongside its interactions with cellular components such as mitochondria and DNA, this paper highlights the extensive damage caused by Cd2+ at the cellular and tissue levels.
evidence.explanation: Draws exactly this edge - from cadmium's absorption and distribution to its interaction with DNA and the resulting cellular damage. Evidence source is OTHER because this is a review article.

edges/4.description: Cadmium delivered to tissues enters cells and, as free intracellular Cd(2+), competes for the structural Zn(II) of zinc-finger domains - the entry point of the genotoxic/carcinogenic arm.

edges/5.description: Circulating cadmium disrupts vascular cholesterol homeostasis via miRNA modulation

edges/6.description: Cd-MT complex released from liver is filtered by glomerulus and reabsorbed by proximal tubule

edges/7.description: Accumulated free cadmium exceeds intracellular metallothionein binding capacity

edges/8.description: Tubular cell injury and death cause loss of reabsorptive function

edges/9.description: Sustained tubular injury leads to tubulointerstitial fibrosis

edges/10.description: Impaired proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption causes phosphaturia

edges/11.description: Loss of proximal tubular reabsorptive function manifests as Fanconi syndrome (renal tubular dysfunction).

edges/12.description: Impaired receptor-mediated reabsorption of low-molecular-weight proteins (beta-2-microglobulin, retinol-binding protein) produces tubular proteinuria.

edges/13.description: Sustained renal phosphate loss lowers serum phosphate, producing hypophosphataemia.

edges/14.description: Chronic hypophosphataemia impairs hydroxyapatite deposition in bone matrix

edges/15.description: Progressive tubulointerstitial nephritis and nephron loss reduce GFR, producing chronic kidney disease.

edges/16.description: Impaired hydroxyapatite deposition in osteoid produces osteomalacia (soft, undermineralized bone).

edges/17.description: Osteomalacia and resulting pathologic fractures produce the severe bone pain characteristic of itai-itai disease.

edges/18.description: A direct bone-cell contribution could compound the established mineralization defect from phosphate wasting, but is not yet demonstrated by the curated evidence.

edges/19.description: A direct bone-cell contribution to reduced bone density is proposed but cannot be separated from nephropathy in the currently curated human evidence.

edges/21.description: Inflammatory cytokines exacerbate tubular cell damage

edges/22.description: Inflammatory mediators compound hepatic oxidative stress

evidence.explanation: The cited work draws exactly this edge: zinc-finger damage in DNA repair proteins as a mechanism of carcinogenesis.

edges/24.description: Impaired repair fidelity allows damage from cadmium-driven oxidative stress and from co-exposures to persist and accumulate, the substrate for malignant transformation.

evidence.snippet: Exposure to cadmium poses a risk for increased cancer incidence and mortality.
evidence.explanation: States the exposure-to-malignancy step this edge asserts, at the level of incidence and mortality.

evidence.snippet: Silver is mixed with cadmium and then used to make silver jewelry. During this process there is a formation of cadmium fumes, and the workers inhale the fumes.
evidence.explanation: Documents cadmium fume formation during silver jewelry manufacture and its inhalation by workers, the occupational inhalational route into the body.

edges/28.description: Industrial processes generate cadmium fume and dust that workers inhale, and inhaled cadmium is the higher-bioavailability route into the body at this node.

evidence.snippet: Heavy metal inhalation is a rare cause of acute lung injury. Among the various heavy metals, cadmium is more commonly known to cause acute lung injury.
evidence.explanation: Directly attributes acute lung injury to inhaled cadmium, the edge from the inhalational exposure to the pulmonary node.

edges/29.description: High-dose fume inhalation injures the alveolar epithelium directly at the portal of entry, without requiring the systemic accumulation that drives the chronic renal and skeletal arms. This is why acute cadmium poisoning presents as a lung disease while chronic poisoning does not.

evidence.snippet: An elderly female farmer with Cd nephropathy residing in a Cd-polluted area in the northern part of the Akita prefecture was identified through hospital-based screening
evidence.explanation: Documents cadmium nephropathy in a farmer living in a cadmium-polluted area, linking residence in a contaminated environment to systemic cadmium disease.

edges/30.description: Cadmium-polluted soil and water enter the food chain, so residents of contaminated areas take cadmium in orally over years. Oral bioavailability is lower than inhalational, but the exposure is continuous.

evidence.snippet: Common risk factors include smoking and alcohol consumption.
evidence.explanation: Lists smoking among the common risk factors for cadmium poisoning. It supports smoking as a recognized route of exposure, not a quantified absorption step.

edges/31.description: Tobacco plants concentrate cadmium from soil, so smoking is an inhalational cadmium source and the dominant non-occupational one. Note the cited sentence establishes smoking as a recognized risk factor for cadmium poisoning; it does not itself measure the absorbed dose.

evidence.snippet: The study also found that low iron stores exacerbate cadmium poisoning.
evidence.explanation: States that low iron stores exacerbate cadmium poisoning, an amplification of the absorption this node describes rather than an independent exposure.

edges/32.description: Low iron stores upregulate the shared divalent metal transporter DMT1, so more of an identical dietary cadmium intake is absorbed. This amplifies absorption rather than providing a source of cadmium, which is why it is a modifier and not a route.

evidence.snippet: The knockdown of ZIP8, ZIP14 or DMT1 by siRNA transfection significantly reduced the uptake of Cd(2+) and Mn(2+) from the apical membrane.
evidence.explanation: siRNA knockdown establishes ZIP8 as a functional route of apical cadmium uptake in proximal tubule cells; no single transporter dominates.

evidence.snippet: ZIP8 and ZIP14 expressed in the S3 segment of proximal tubules play significant roles in the absorption of Cd(2+) and Mn(2+) in the kidney
evidence.explanation: Localises the transporter to the S3 segment, the nephron site where cadmium accumulates and where the proximal tubular injury of this disease begins.

evidence.snippet: the single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) variant A391T (rs13107325) is associated with numerous human traits
evidence.explanation: Establishes that a common functional variant of this transporter exists and is phenotypically consequential. PARTIAL because the traits studied are blood pressure and insulin resistance, not cadmium handling - the link to cadmium susceptibility is inferred from the transporter's role, not measured.

genes/0.notes: Cadmium poisoning is an acquired toxic disorder with no causal gene, so every entry in this section is a modifier of toxicokinetics or of detoxification capacity. The common A391T (rs13107325) variant reduces ZIP8 transport activity; its consequence for human cadmium handling specifically has not been measured, so no directional susceptibility claim is curated for it here.

evidence.snippet: ZIP8 and ZIP14 expressed in the S3 segment of proximal tubules play significant roles in the absorption of Cd(2+) and Mn(2+) in the kidney
evidence.explanation: Directly assigns ZIP14 a significant role in renal cadmium absorption at the segment where cadmium concentrates.

evidence.snippet: The knockdown of ZIP8, ZIP14 or DMT1 by siRNA transfection significantly reduced the uptake of Cd(2+) and Mn(2+) from the apical membrane.
evidence.explanation: Establishes DMT1 as a functional cadmium uptake route in proximal tubule cells, complementing its better-known intestinal role.

evidence.snippet: uptake of free Cd(2+) has been demonstrated for the Fe(2+)/H(+) cotransporter divalent metal transporter 1.
evidence.explanation: Identifies DMT1 as the iron cotransporter that also carries free cadmium, the shared-route mechanism behind the iron-deficiency interaction.

evidence.snippet: Cadmium accumulates in the renal cortex by the long-term exposure along with increased concentrations of metallothionein, an important protein for protection from cadmium toxicity.
evidence.explanation: States metallothionein's protective role and its co-accumulation with cadmium in the renal cortex, the target organ of chronic toxicity.

evidence.snippet: some individuals have lower metallothionein levels despite increased cadmium accumulation in the kidneys
evidence.explanation: Documents the inter-individual variation in metallothionein response that makes this a susceptibility modifier rather than a uniform protective factor.

genes/3.notes: Curated as a MODIFIER rather than a SUSCEPTIBILITY locus because the cited evidence documents inter-individual variation in metallothionein level at a given renal cadmium burden; specific MT1A/MT2A promoter variants and their effect sizes are not established in the cited source. MT2A is curated separately.

evidence.snippet: some individuals have lower metallothionein levels despite increased cadmium accumulation in the kidneys
evidence.explanation: Same inter-individual metallothionein variation applies to the MT2A isoform; the cited work does not resolve the isoforms separately.

evidence.snippet: The treatment plan includes the use of chelating agents to reduce cadmium levels in the body and antibiotics to maintain the patient's condition.
evidence.explanation: Systematic review confirms chelating agents as part of standard cadmium poisoning treatment.

evidence.snippet: Conventional chelation therapy, when used long-term, can lead to renal and gastrointestinal diseases.
evidence.explanation: Review highlights significant limitations of conventional chelation therapy, noting long-term use can itself cause renal and gastrointestinal toxicity.

evidence.snippet: The renal deposition of Cd increased on BAL (2,3-dimercaptopropanol) treatment a short time (1/2 hr) after Cd exposure.
evidence.explanation: Rat data are the basis for avoiding early BAL in cadmium exposure; marked PARTIAL because this is an animal redistribution finding, not a clinical outcome study.

evidence.snippet: if BAL was administered 24 hr after Cd exposure, it could mobilize Cd from hepatic MT and increase the biliary excretion of Cd without any increase in renal Cd concentration
evidence.explanation: The same rat study bounds the caution: the renal-redistribution effect is timing-dependent and not observed once metallothionein has been induced.

treatments/0.description: Chelating agents (CaNa2-EDTA, DMSA, DMPS) are used to bind and promote urinary excretion of cadmium. Effectiveness is limited due to cadmium's tight binding to metallothionein and intracellular sequestration. BAL (dimercaprol) is generally avoided: in rat experiments BAL given shortly after cadmium exposure increased renal cadmium deposition, redistributing the metal toward the critical target organ. The same work shows the effect is timing-dependent — BAL given 24 hours after exposure, once metallothionein has been induced, mobilized hepatic cadmium into bile without raising renal cadmium — so this is an animal-derived caution about early administration rather than a demonstrated clinical contraindication in humans.

evidence.snippet: They were initiated on neutral phosphate and calcitriol. On follow-up, they reported significant reduction in severity of symptoms.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates effectiveness of phosphate supplementation (combined with calcitriol) for cadmium-induced osteomalacia.

treatments/1.description: Neutral phosphate supplements to correct hypophosphataemia from renal phosphate wasting. Phosphate replacement is essential for treating the underlying metabolic defect driving cadmium-induced osteomalacia and results in significant symptom improvement when combined with calcitriol.

evidence.snippet: They were initiated on neutral phosphate and calcitriol. On follow-up, they reported significant reduction in severity of symptoms.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates effectiveness of calcitriol for cadmium-induced osteomalacia.

evidence.snippet: for patients with osteochondropathy, supplementation with calcium and vitamin D is recommended.
evidence.explanation: Systematic review recommends calcium and vitamin D supplementation for skeletal complications.

evidence.snippet: typical severe osteomalacia, which responded well initially to calcium and vitamin D treatment.
evidence.explanation: Case report confirms initial good response to calcium and vitamin D in cadmium-induced osteomalacia.

treatments/2.description: Calcitriol (active vitamin D) supplementation to treat osteomalacia, bypassing the impaired renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation caused by cadmium nephrotoxicity. Calcium supplementation may also be required to address secondary hyperparathyroidism and calcium malabsorption.

evidence.snippet: For patients with concurrent lung and kidney involvement, mechanical ventilation and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) may be required.
evidence.explanation: Systematic review confirms need for ICU-level care in severe acute cadmium poisoning.

treatments/3.description: For acute cadmium inhalation with pulmonary involvement, intensive care including mechanical ventilation for ARDS and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) for concurrent renal failure may be required.

evidence.snippet: Therefore, an early diagnosis and prevention of further exposure are important.
evidence.explanation: Emphasizes the importance of preventing further cadmium exposure given lack of effective treatment.

evidence.snippet: regulatory agencies and policy makers ought to survey the silver industry and ensure that the metals used are within permissible safe limits of exposure.
evidence.explanation: Calls for occupational regulation to prevent cadmium exposure in the silver industry.

treatments/4.description: Removal from cadmium exposure source is essential. Occupational hygiene measures include adequate ventilation, personal protective equipment, and workplace monitoring. Public health interventions include environmental remediation of contaminated soil and water, and regulatory limits on cadmium in food and consumer products.

evidence.snippet: We will present a case of cadmium induced peripheral neuropathy, nephropathy, and decreased bone density.
evidence.explanation: The available human observation couples reduced bone density with nephropathy in the same patient, which is exactly why the question of a direct-versus-renal route remains open.

open_questions/0.rationale: Cadmium-exposed patients who develop bone disease characteristically also have proximal tubular injury with phosphate wasting, so clinical observations of reduced bone density cannot separate a direct bone-cell effect from the established renal route. No osteoblast-culture or animal skeletal evidence is currently curated in this entry, so the direct arm is recorded as an unresolved mechanism rather than an asserted one.

evidence.snippet: most disease linked ASPA gene variants lead to a structural destabilization
evidence.explanation: Recent review supports ASPA protein destabilization as a common mechanism.

steps/1.description: Many disease-linked ASPA missense variants destabilize the aspartoacylase protein, promoting misfolding and proteasomal degradation and thereby reducing active enzyme abundance.

evidence.snippet: deficiency of the cytosolic aspartoacylase (ASPA) enzyme
evidence.explanation: Mechanistic review directly identifies aspartoacylase deficiency.

evidence.snippet: ASPA acts to hydrolyze N-acetylaspartate (NAA) into l-aspartate and acetate
evidence.explanation: Mouse model study describes the enzymatic reaction blocked in Canavan disease.

steps/2.description: Loss of ASPA activity impairs the cytosolic/oligodendroglial hydrolysis of N-acetyl-L-aspartate to acetate and aspartate, initiating the core biochemical disease cascade.

evidence.snippet: Deficiency of the enzyme aspartoacylase and the accumulation of N-acetylaspartic acid

evidence.snippet: We identified a homozygous stop-gain variant in LRRC32 (c.1630C>T; p.(Arg544Ter)) in two families with developmental delay, cleft palate, and proliferative retinopathy.
evidence.explanation: The discovery report establishes the homozygous truncating LRRC32 genotype in the affected families.

evidence.snippet: The p.327Ile > Thr is likely to destabilize the LRR structure, both by introducing a polar residue into a hydrophobic pocket and by, at the same time, introducing an unoccupied cavity that destabilizes the structure.
evidence.explanation: Structural modelling on the GARP crystal structure predicts destabilisation of the leucine-rich-repeat ectodomain by the missense allele; this is a prediction, not a measured loss of function.

steps/1.description: Biallelic LRRC32 variants remove or destabilise GARP, a type I transmembrane leucine-rich-repeat protein whose large ectodomain docks latent TGF-beta at the cell surface. The discovery families carry a homozygous stop-gain, p.(Arg544Ter), which truncates the protein before the transmembrane domain; the fourth patient carries a homozygous missense substitution, p.Ile327Thr, predicted on the GARP:latent-TGF-beta1 crystal structure to destabilise the leucine-rich-repeat solenoid. Neither allele has been shown biochemically to abolish GARP function, so loss of function is inferred from genotype, structure, and phenotype rather than demonstrated directly.

evidence.snippet: We show that GARP or LRRC32, a leucine-rich repeat molecule of unknown function, is critical for tethering TGF-beta to the cell surface.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the tethering function that is lost when GARP is absent.

evidence.snippet: In vitro studies confirmed that GARP and TGFβ3 directly interact and that GARP is indispensable for the surface expression of membrane-associated latent TGFβ3.
evidence.explanation: Extends the tethering requirement to TGF-beta3, the isoform that matters for palatal fusion.

steps/2.description: GARP binds the latency-associated peptide of pro-TGF-beta through intermolecular disulphide bonds and holds the resulting latent complex on the plasma membrane. Without GARP the latent complex is not presented at the cell surface. This step was worked out in regulatory T cells and platelets; the same requirement was later shown for membrane-associated latent TGF-beta3 in the palatal epithelium.

evidence.snippet: Taken together, LRRC32 loss of function variants result in GARP dysfunction and consequently abnormal maturation and inactivation of TGF-β.
evidence.explanation: The authors state the mechanistic conclusion that the disease-causing step is failure of TGF-beta maturation and activation.

evidence.snippet: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) suppress immune cells within close proximity by activating latent TGF-β1 presented by GARP (glycoprotein A repetitions predominant) to integrin αVβ8 on their surface.
evidence.explanation: Names the integrin-dependent activation step that GARP presentation enables; loss of GARP removes the substrate for that step.

steps/3.description: With latent TGF-beta no longer presented at the cell surface, the integrin alphaVbeta6/alphaVbeta8-dependent release of active cytokine cannot proceed where GARP-expressing cells would normally supply it. The defect is in local, cell-contact-dependent availability of active TGF-beta rather than in synthesis of the cytokine or in the receptor-SMAD machinery itself.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, we observed decreased apoptosis and SMAD2 phosphorylation in the medial edge epithelial cells of the palatal shelf of GARP KO embryos at embryonic day 14.5 (E14.5), indicating a defect in the TGFβ signaling pathway in the GARP-null developing palates.
evidence.explanation: The two measurements that define this node, made in the GARP knockout mouse.

steps/4.description: Fusion of the secondary palate requires TGF-beta3 signalling in the medial edge epithelium, whose cells normally undergo programmed cell death and epithelial-mesenchymal transformation to remove the midline epithelial seam. In GARP-null mouse embryos both SMAD2 phosphorylation and apoptosis in this cell population are reduced at embryonic day 14.5. This node is characterised entirely in the mouse; no human palatal tissue has been examined.

evidence.snippet: Unexpectedly, the GARP KO mice died within 24 h after birth and exhibited defective palatogenesis without apparent abnormalities in other major organs.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that removing GARP is by itself sufficient to break palatogenesis in vivo.

evidence.snippet: the embryonic primary and secondary palatal shelves develop as outgrowths from the medial nasal and maxillary prominences, respectively, remodel and fuse to form the intact roof of the oral cavity
evidence.explanation: A developmental-biology review describing the normal process whose failure this node names.

steps/5.description: The secondary palatal shelves grow out from the maxillary prominences, elevate above the tongue, appose at the midline, and fuse. Loss of the TGF-beta signal in the medial edge epithelium leaves the midline seam intact and the shelves unfused, producing an isolated cleft of the secondary palate without cleft lip.

evidence.snippet: The transforming growth factor-beta (TGFβ) signaling pathway is essential for palatogenesis and retinal development.
evidence.explanation: States the premise on which the retinal arm of this syndrome is interpreted.

evidence.snippet: We report now that eyes of Tgfbeta2/Tgfbeta3 double-deficient mice display severe alterations in the morphology of the retina, lens, and cornea.
evidence.explanation: Independent evidence that loss of TGF-beta ligand disrupts retinal morphogenesis, supporting the direction of this node although the model removes the ligands rather than the GARP tether.

evidence.snippet: In Tgfbeta2(-/-) Tgfbeta3(-/-) and Tgfbeta2(-/-) Tgfbeta3(+/-) littermates the retina was consistently detached from the underlying pigment epithelium.
evidence.explanation: Retinal detachment in TGF-beta-deficient mice is the closest model counterpart to the tractional retinal complications seen in patients.

steps/6.description: TGF-beta isoforms are expressed in the developing retina and are required for normal retinal morphogenesis; combined Tgfb2/Tgfb3 deficiency in mice produces gross retinal, lens, and corneal abnormality with retinal detachment. In CPPRDD the ocular disease is a progressive, childhood-onset vitreoretinopathy with a persistent hyaloid remnant, straightened retinal vessels, a thickened vitreous adherent to the peripheral retina, and traction with secondary retinal tears. How deficient GARP-dependent TGF-beta activation produces this specific vitreoretinal picture is not established.

evidence.snippet: First, mouse studies have uncovered roles of GARP only in palatogenesis, immune tolerance and cancer immune evasion (Fig. 1), but these three cases suggest that GARP may play other roles including in development of the central nervous system and the retina.
evidence.explanation: The commentary explicitly identifies a central nervous system role for GARP as a possibility raised by the patients and not previously demonstrated.

steps/7.description: Developmental delay is present in every published patient, and brain imaging in the discovery series showed ventriculomegaly and corpus callosum abnormalities. No GARP-dependent step in brain development has been identified, in mouse or in human tissue; the Garp-null mouse dies within a day of birth and no neurodevelopmental phenotype has been reported in it.

evidence.snippet: First, mouse studies have uncovered roles of GARP only in palatogenesis, immune tolerance and cancer immune evasion (Fig. 1), but these three cases suggest that GARP may play other roles including in development of the central nervous system and the retina.

genes/0.notes: Two alleles are published. The homozygous nonsense c.1630C>T p.(Arg544Ter) segregated in the two families of the 2019 discovery series; it truncates GARP before the transmembrane domain and is predicted to leave a soluble product, but neither the abundance of that product nor its residual activity has been measured. The homozygous missense c.980T>C p.Ile327Thr in the fourth patient was classified a variant of uncertain significance under ACMG criteria (PM2, PP3, PP4) and was supported by structural modelling rather than by a functional assay. No ClinGen gene-disease validity assertion for LRRC32 was found in the local structured-source cache. Because both reports come from the same country and share a senior author, the four patients are not four independent ascertainments in the usual sense.

treatments/1.description: Prophylactic argon laser photocoagulation of the peripheral retina to wall off tractional lesions and prevent retinal detachment. The reported patient required a second treatment a year later when a new vitreoretinal traction appeared. This is a single-patient experience, not evidence of efficacy in this syndrome.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Laser treats the tractional and proliferative consequence in the retina; it does not act on the GARP-TGF-beta lesion upstream of it.

treatments/2.description: Repeated fundus examination and optical coherence tomography. The one patient followed in detail developed a new peripheral vitreoretinal traction within a year of his first laser treatment, which is the observation that motivates surveillance rather than one-off assessment. No screening interval has been established for this syndrome.

treatments/3.description: Early intervention and rehabilitation for the global developmental delay. Nothing specific to this syndrome has been published; the sources establish that delay is present in every patient, not what should be done about it.

evidence.snippet: Two siblings (III-1 and III-5) were heterozygous and three siblings (III-3, III-4, and III-6) did not carry the variant
evidence.explanation: Sibling carrier testing in the reported kindred, which is the counselling action offered to at-risk relatives once an allele is known.

treatments/4.description: Autosomal recessive recurrence risk counselling for the family, with carrier testing where an allele is known. Both published kindreds were consanguineous, and segregation testing in the 2022 family returned the expected mix of heterozygous and non-carrier siblings, which is the concrete question carrier testing is offered to answer. The diagnostic testing that makes counselling possible is curated under `diagnosis:` rather than here.
